The embryonic development of Chelidonichthys lucerna begins with the release of small, pelagic eggs that undergo rapid cleavage. At the time of chorion rupture, the prolarvae that emerge measure approximately 0.309 cm  in total length, a size that reflects the modest yolk reserves characteristic of this species. When eggs are incubated at a stable water temperature of 13.5 °C [T = 13.5 °C], the time required to reach this hatching event has been documented as 4.79 days . Shortly after eclosion, the yolk-sac larvae remain lecithotrophic, subsisting entirely on endogenous nutrients during a brief endotrophic phase. The transition to exogenous feeding occurs concurrently with the completion of yolk absorption, and the age at which these free-swimming larvae become truly independent, marking the biological age at birth into the pelagic environment, has been recorded at 15 days [ab = 15 days] under those same controlled thermal conditions at a temperature of 13.5 °C [T = 13.5 °C]. This relatively protracted yolk-sac phase compared to some other triglids may confer an advantage in buffering against sporadic prey availability during the early larval period.

As the pelagic larvae grow, they undergo considerable morphological transformation before settling to a demersal lifestyle. Juvenile individuals gradually approach the size at which they become reproductively competent, although the timing of this transition differs between the sexes. For females, the total length at which puberty is first observed has been determined to be 15.3 cm [Lp = 15.3 cm], while males typically attain sexual maturity at a somewhat larger body size of 17.6 cm [Lp = 17.6 cm]. This sexual dimorphism in maturation length is a common pattern among benthic marine fishes and likely reflects differential energetic demands associated with gamete production. The ultimate total length that a Tub gurnard can achieve over its lifetime has been recorded at 61 cm [Li = 61 cm], a respectable maximum size within the family Triglidae that positions this species as one of the larger members of its genus. Comparative data from trawl surveys indicate that individuals reaching this asymptotic length are relatively uncommon, likely due to the combined pressures of fishing mortality and natural senescence.

The maximum wet weight corresponding to the largest individuals of Chelidonichthys lucerna has been reported at 6000 grams [Wwi = 6000 grams], placing the species among the heavier-bodied gurnards in the northeastern Atlantic and Mediterranean. This considerable adult mass reflects a life history strategy oriented toward achieving a large body size before investing heavily in reproduction. Individuals of Tub gurnard are iteroparous, spawning multiple times across several seasons. The longevity of this species has been examined through otolith-based age estimation, and the maximum lifespan recorded under natural conditions at a water temperature of 13.5 °C [T = 13.5 °C] is approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years]. This relatively extended lifespan for a demersal teleost is consistent with a growth pattern that prioritizes somatic investment during the early and middle years, deferring peak reproductive output until the fish have reached a substantial size. Such a schedule is typical of species that experience moderate natural mortality once they attain a size refuge from predation.

Females of Chelidonichthys lucerna are batch spawners, releasing multiple clutches of pelagic eggs over an extended spawning season that spans the spring and summer months. The fecundity per reproductive event has been quantified as 120,000 to 200,000 eggs per batch [N_R_i = 120,000 to 200,000 eggs per batch], a high fecundity that compensates for the substantial mortality experienced during the planktonic larval phase. Spawning frequency is similarly elevated, with females producing approximately 15 to 20 batches each year [F_R_i = approximately 15 to 20 batches each year]. This combination of large clutch sizes and high batch frequency results in a substantial annual reproductive output, a strategy well-suited to an environment where early life survival is highly variable and unpredictable. The reproductive biology of this species appears optimized for maximizing fecundity over the course of a single season, rather than producing a smaller number of well-provisioned offspring. Such a pattern is common among marine demersal spawners that release buoyant, unprotected eggs into the water column.

Feeding ecology of Tub gurnard is characterized by a benthic, carnivorous diet dominated by crustaceans, mollusks, and small demersal fishes. The species uses its modified pectoral fin rays as chemosensory organs to detect buried prey, a behavior that allows it to forage effectively on soft sediment bottoms. Growth rates during the juvenile stage are relatively rapid, with individuals reaching the female size at puberty within two to three years, reflecting a developmental trajectory that balances the energetic costs of rapid somatic growth against the need to accumulate sufficient lipid reserves for successful reproduction. The value for total length at birth, measured immediately following the completion of the yolk-sac stage, has been estimated at 0.485 cm [Lb = 0.485 cm], which is notably larger than the hatching length due to significant growth during the endotrophic larval phase. This increase in size prior to first feeding is a critical period that reduces vulnerability to starvation and predation as the larvae transition to exogenous nutrition. Overall, the life history of Chelidonichthys lucerna exemplifies a K-selected strategy within a fecund, pelagic-spawning teleost.
